definition: The study of how living things affect each other and interact with their environment.
A limited area with all its organisms and their environment, e.g. a lake, a forest or a tree stump.
All individuals of the same species living in a certain area, e.g. all perch in a lake.
All populations (plants, animals, fungi and bacteria) living together in an ecosystem.
All the ecosystems on Earth together – the part of the planet where there is life.
Plants and algae build glucose from carbon dioxide and water using light energy. Oxygen is formed: carbon dioxide + water + light energy → glucose + oxygen.
An organism that makes its own food through photosynthesis, e.g. plants and algae. It comes first in every food chain.
The cells break down glucose using oxygen and release energy: glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water + energy. Happens in almost all organisms.
A model that uses arrows to show who eats whom, from producer to top consumer.
An organism that gets its food by eating other organisms. It can be a primary consumer, a secondary consumer and so on.
The organism at the end of a food chain that is not eaten by any other animal.
Many food chains in an ecosystem that are linked to each other.
A model showing that there is most living material at the bottom (the producers) and least at the top. Only about 10 % of the food passes on to the next level.
Organisms that live on dead plants and animals and break them down into soil, e.g. fungi, bacteria and earthworms.
When a substance, e.g. carbon, water or nutrients, goes round in nature and is used again and again.
Substances that plants take up from the soil with water and need in order to grow, e.g. nitrogen and phosphorus.
The way a species lives in the ecosystem: what it eats, where and when. Species with different niches avoid competing.
That there are many different species, many types of habitat and great variation within species.
Loose material on top of the bedrock that you can dig in, e.g. till, sand and clay.
Sweden's most common soil type. A mixture of boulders, stones, gravel, sand and clay left behind by the ice sheet.
Dead leaves, needles, twigs and animals lying on top of the ground that have not yet been broken down.
The upper part of the ground, under the leaf litter, that has been affected by climate and organisms. It contains humus.
Small organisms that float freely in the water. Phytoplankton are producers; zooplankton eat them.
When the pH falls in soil and water, mainly because of emissions of sulphur and nitrogen oxides. Sensitive species die.
When soil and water get too many nutrients. Algae and plants grow strongly and oxygen shortage can occur.
Water that is saltier than fresh water but less salty than salt water, about 0.05–3 % salt. The Baltic Sea is brackish.
What nature gives us for free, e.g. pollination, clean water, oxygen, fish and timber.
A poisonous substance that breaks down very slowly and builds up in the food chain, e.g. DDT, PCB and mercury.
